title: Pasta all'Amatriciana
subtitle: Rigatoni with cured pork, tomato, and chilli
excerpt: Amatriciana is one of Rome's four canonical pasta sauces: a simple combination of cured pork, tomato, and chilli that comes together in under 30 minutes. The pork renders its fat into the pan, which becomes the base of the sauce. It is deeply savoury and a little spiky from the chilli.
sourceNotes: Amatriciana originates from the town of Amatrice in Lazio and is one of Rome's four canonical pasta sauces. The original uses guanciale and pecorino romano; pork belly and parmesan are practical substitutes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the sauce in portions for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the sauce and freeze half.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce (without pasta) can be made up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated.

content.text: The pork does most of the work in amatriciana: it needs to render slowly so that the fat becomes a cooking medium rather than a greasy puddle. Take the heat low and give it time. Traditionally this dish uses pecorino romano rather than parmesan: use pecorino if you can find it. A splash of red wine vinegar added to the pan after the pork crisps up adds welcome acidity. Use rigatoni or another large ridged pasta shape that can trap the chunky sauce inside the tubes.
Put a large pan of well-salted water on to boil for the pasta. It should taste pleasantly of the sea.

Place the pork belly lardons in a cold frying pan with the olive oil. Set the heat to medium-low and cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat has rendered and the pork is golden and crisp. Starting in a cold pan helps the fat render gently rather than seizing up.
Add the chilli flakes to the pan and cook for 30 seconds, letting them bloom in the rendered fat. If using red wine vinegar, add a small splash now and let it bubble away for 30 seconds.

Add the tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with a wooden spoon. Season with a little salt (the pork is already salty, so go carefully). Simmer over a medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes until the sauce has thickened and the oil has risen to the surface in small pools.
Cook the rigatoni in the boiling water according to the packet instructions, taking it out 1 minute before the stated time. Reserve a large mug of pasta cooking water before draining.

Drain the pasta and add it directly to the frying pan with the sauce. Toss over a medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, adding splashes of pasta water to loosen the sauce as needed. The starchy water helps the sauce cling to the pasta.
Serve immediately in warmed bowls with grated parmesan or pecorino on top. A drizzle of olive oil over each bowl is optional but good.

items.symptom: The pork is rubbery rather than crisp
items.cause: The heat was too high and the fat seized rather than rendering out slowly.
items.fix: Start the pork in a cold pan over a low heat next time. If this batch is rubbery, continue cooking on a medium heat and give it more time: the fat will eventually render and the pork will crisp.

items.symptom: The sauce tastes very sharp and acidic
items.cause: The tomatoes did not cook long enough, or the tinned tomatoes were acidic.
items.fix: Continue simmering the sauce for another 5 to 10 minutes. If it is still sharp, add a pinch of sugar and stir through.

items.symptom: The pasta and sauce are not coming together
items.cause: The pasta was drained without reserving water, or it was added to the sauce too dry.
items.fix: Add pasta cooking water a splash at a time while tossing over the heat. The starch in the water emulsifies the sauce and helps it coat every piece of pasta.
